sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

content.text:
Case F45: segment the fibrous soft-tissue tumor on this T2-weighted MRI.

Volume: 261x261x435 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case F45 | sequence T2 | shape (i,j,k)=(261, 261, 435) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: fibrous soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).

content.thinking:
I'm working out the coronal slice orientation — lower index appears posterior, higher index anterior, with the femur shaft visible around coronal 130 and the knee/patella region toward 160-170. I'm also noting bright tissue superior to the mask at coronal 80-100.

The bright cap-shaped tissue above the mass could represent the tumor's superior extent, possibly myxoid or fluid-like signal, or alternatively peritumoral edema within the hamstring muscles — in axial 232 it looks layered like muscle fascicles, suggesting biceps femoris edema, though heterogeneous desmoid tumor signal is also possible. I want to check axial 235 and 260 more closely to clarify.

content.text: axial 245/435 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 7/40, prompts 1/15

content.thinking:
I'm noting a bright lobulated mass posterior to the femur with a heterogeneous swirl pattern, suggestive of a fibrous or desmoid-type tumor, while a nearby lateral region with intermediate signal and striations could represent either tumor extension or edematous muscle rather than the vastus.

Checking the sagittal series now, I see the mass may actually be bilobed — a lower encapsulated heterogeneous portion and a brighter upper component extending superiorly along the posterior femur, so I want to view sagittal 140 with the overlay to confirm continuity between the two.

content.text: sagittal 140/261 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 8/40, prompts 1/15

content.thinking:
Looking at the sagittal view, I notice the heterogeneous encapsulated mass has a bright superior extension that tapers off, which could be fluid, edema, or the tumor's own superior pole within a fascial compartment. There's also some heterogeneous tissue inferior to the mask that might represent additional tumor extent. This pattern is consistent with a fibrous tumor like a desmoid.

Desmoid tumors often show a "fascial tail" sign, and the tapering bright superior part could represent this fascial extension, which annotation rules say should be included if contiguous with the mass along fascia. I'm weighing whether this bright region is edema (less common in desmoids) versus a more cellular, less fibrous part of the tumor itself, given its lobulated borders and swirled internal pattern seen on the axial slice. Looking across other axial levels, the bright posterior region near the femur also shows similar lobulated, well-defined contours and brightness matching the main mass periphery, suggesting it's likely part of the same lesion that annotators would have included in a full segmentation.

I'm now checking whether the sagittal view shows a clear separation between the main mass and the superior bright region, since there's no obvious dark boundary line posteriorly, and the bright area seems to extend continuously upward for several centimeters before fading out in the more superior axial slices. I also want to check the coronal images to see how this bright cap wraps around the main mass, which should help clarify whether it's a true extension or a separate structure.

Looking more closely at the signal pattern, I'm considering whether this cap could represent edema rather than tumor extension, since fluid/edema and tumor can look similarly bright but edema often shows a feathery, ill-defined infiltrative pattern into muscle rather than sharp lobulated margins. The posterior part of the bright region does show well-defined, rounded borders that look more like tumor, while the lateral portion has striated edges more consistent with surrounding edema or infiltration, so I want to check another axial level to confirm this distinction.

content.text: axial 225/435 | crop full | marks none | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 9/40, prompts 1/15
axial 272/435 | crop full | marks none | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 10/40, prompts 1/15

content.thinking:
At axial 225, I'm looking at the superior pole of the mass — a small rounded lesion with a dark rim, surrounded by broad feathery bright tissue that appears to be within the adjacent muscle (adductor magnus/hamstrings) with a striated pattern, suggesting either edema or tumor infiltration. There's also a separate bright blob anterolateral near the femur at this same level that looks distinct from the main mass.

I'm considering whether this could be myxofibrosarcoma, which characteristically shows a "tail sign" — curvilinear myxoid infiltration along fascial planes with high T2 signal — rather than simple edema, especially since at axial 272 the posterior bright region is very intense, homogeneous, and lobulated, more consistent with fluid or myxoid tumor than reactive edema.

Looking at sagittal 140 again, the bright region superior to the mass sits within fascial boundaries, tapering superiorly without striations, suggesting a filled compartment of myxoid tumor rather than muscle; but at axial 245 I notice a whorled, striated pattern resembling pennate muscle fibers, which complicates that interpretation. I'm now wondering if the tumor is multilobulated, extending into bright regions both above and below the main mass, and leaning toward this being a case from a fibrous soft-tissue tumor dataset, possibly desmoid-type fibromatosis.

The fan-shaped bright region at axial 232, radiating posteromedially from the linea aspera with visible streaks, matches the anatomy of the short head of biceps femoris or adductor magnus — raising the question of whether this diffuse high signal represents edema or actual desmoid infiltration into the muscle itself.

Higher up, at axial 272, I notice a very bright, homogeneous area posterior to the femur with a lobulated margin, fading out by 304. There's also a separate bright lobule anterolateral to the femur at 225, plus another isolated bright blob seen on the sagittal view, so there appear to be multiple distinct components rather than one simple mass. Given the encapsulated, heterogeneous appearance with a dark rim, I'm weighing possibilities like a solitary fibrous tumor, though those usually lack surrounding edema, which doesn't quite fit here.

Myxofibrosarcoma seems more consistent: it's typically multinodular with high T2 signal, infiltrative tails along fascial planes, and peritumoral edema, which matches the surrounding bright "tail" region better. I'm also recalling that in some soft-tissue sarcoma imaging datasets, like the Vallières TCIA dataset, tumor contours drawn on T2-fat-saturated sequences may have included peritumoral edema rather than just the solid tumor itself.

Given that uncertainty, I'm trying to estimate the volumetric impact: the main mass is around 555 mL, and the questionable bright superior region might add roughly 100 mL. Whether I include or exclude this region relative to the ground truth could shift the Dice score by about 0.08 in either direction, so the error seems roughly symmetric either way—I want to look more closely at the sagittal and coronal views to judge this better.

Looking at the overview images again, I'm checking whether the bright region shows mass effect (convex, lobulated borders displacing structures) versus following normal muscle architecture, trying to trace exactly which muscle compartment—biceps femoris versus adductor magnus—the bright signal corresponds to near the femur.

Mapping out the thigh anatomy at that level: quadriceps anteriorly, vessels medial to the femur, trying to pin down exact pixel coordinates to establish medial versus lateral orientation given uncertain right/left labeling.

That fluid-like homogeneity with a lobulated, sharply defined posterior margin seems more consistent with a tumor component than edema, and the sagittal view shows it tapering continuously from the main mass, like a tail sign. The feathery margin around the small capsule nodule at 225 looks like a transition zone, so I want to check the sagittal images further inferiorly too.

Below the mask, there's heterogeneous brightness, and the bright blobs near the inferior end on sagittal 98 in the popliteal region are probably joint fluid or a Baker's cyst rather than tumor. I'm thinking I should test a positive point inside the superior bright region on axial 260 to see how the model responds, but first I want to reconsider the coronal view, where that bright cap above the mask wraps the superior pole with a smooth, convex margin extending roughly 50mm up.

In coronal 80 the bright region above the mask has a fairly sharp border, bounded laterally by a dark fascia line — this pattern resembles a bright cap of edema at a tumor pole, something I've seen with myxofibrosarcoma. I'm leaning toward including it as contiguous extension, though I'm wary since edema isn't normal anatomy but also isn't clearly lesion tissue either, so I want to zoom into axial 255 for texture before placing marker points on axial 258.

content.text: axial 258/435 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 11/40, prompts 1/15

content.thinking:
At this slice, the bright lobulated region appears sharply demarcated posteriorly by a dark fascial line, with intermediate signal muscle showing striations in between — this looks like fluid within a fascial plane or possibly a lesion, with streaks tracking along the femur. The lateral area shows intermediate signal with internal dark curvilinear bands.

This is genuinely ambiguous. Comparing it to the main encapsulated mass with its heterogeneous bright internal signal, the superior bright region is brighter and more homogeneous, but the whorled dark bands seen more superiorly actually resemble the classic low-signal band pattern of desmoid tumors, which strengthens that possibility. Given the instruction to capture extension along fascia contiguous with the mass, I'll include the bright superior extension but leave out the feathery intermediate muscle regions, marking positive points at coordinates on this slice.

content.thinking: I should keep the response brief and to the point.

content.text:
I saved the mask for the fibrous tumor at medium confidence (version v3). The main uncertainty is whether the bright tissue above the mass is tumor or swelling (edema) in the surrounding muscle; I left it out.

**What's in the mask:** a large mass in the back of the thigh, behind the thighbone, with a dark outer capsule and a patchy, mixed-brightness interior. It runs about 15 cm from top to bottom (axial slices 89–239) and measures 595.7 mL. Five positive points on the slice where it is largest produced the first mask (555 mL). I then widened it by 1 mm because the outline sat just inside the dark capsule, which should count as part of the lesion. That added 40 mL.

**What I left out:** above the mass (about axial 220–300) there is a large, very bright region bounded by the thin sheets of tissue that separate muscles. A positive point there nearly doubled the mask to 1034 mL. It also spread into normal-looking grey muscle up to axial 342. I undid it because:
- At its lowest point, the capsule closes around a small round nodule that sits inside this bright tissue, so the bright tissue is outside the capsule.
- Inside, it shows fan-shaped streaks that follow the muscle fibres, which looks like swollen muscle rather than a mass pushing tissue aside.

If whoever drew the reference outline counted it as tumor that has grown into the muscle, my mask is missing roughly 300–480 mL.
